unit.title: Perform basic welding using manual metal arc welding process (MMAW)

summary: At Level 3 this unit takes manual metal arc welding (MMAW) from making a sound weld to planning, controlling and checking MMAW work. You will work to a welding procedure specification (WPS), lead safe set-ups, understand power sources and the welding circuit, choose and control electrodes, prepare joints and make multi-run fillet and butt welds. You will also do the welder's calculations, find and prevent faults, inspect and test welds, keep records and supervise trainees.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **manual metal arc welding (MMAW)**, also called stick welding or SMAW, of carbon steel. At Level 2 you learned to strike an arc and run sound beads. At Level 3 you are expected to **work to a WPS**, make multi-run welds, understand why each setting matters, check other people's work, and lead a bay or a small site job safely.

MMAW is still the most widely used welding process in Jamaica: gates and grilles, tank stands, building steel, trailers, farm and factory repairs, and site work where a portable or engine-driven machine is all there is. A Level 3 welder is the person others ask: which electrode, what current, why it cracked, whether it passes.
**Who it is for:** Level 3 trainees and welders who can already make basic MMAW welds, and who now plan the work, check it and guide others.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at Level 3
rows: Read a WPS and stay inside it; know what a supervisor checks; know why qualification matters.
Control shock, fume, fire, confined-space and site hazards for yourself and others; check a bay before arcs are struck.
Explain power-source types, the drooping output, duty cycle, cables, polarity and arc blow.
Choose the class and size for a job; store and issue electrodes so the right, dry ones are used.
Prepare single-V butts and tee joints to the WPS, with the right gaps, root faces, tacks and tabs.
Weld roots, hot passes, fills and caps, and three-run fillets, in the positions the job needs.
Heat input, travel speed, arc time, throat and leg sizes, duty cycle, quantities and costs in J$.
Name faults, their causes and cures, and how each is found.
Inspect by eye and gauge; know the destructive and non-destructive tests; record repairs.
Check set-ups, coach trainees from the fault they show, and report.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on procedures, safety, machines, electrodes, calculations, welding method, faults, testing and supervision.

A **written paper**: short answers (exact terms such as arc blow, cap, reinforcement, quiver, run-off tab, heat-affected zone) with calculations; and longer answers on the WPS, electrodes, site safety, heat input, multi-run welds, defects, testing, arc blow, electrode control and repairs.

**Group practical tasks**: three-run tee fillet welds to a WPS with a fillet break test and weld record; and single-V butt welds in 10 mm plate with visual inspection, bend or nick-break tests and an inspection report.

blocks.note: At this level, answers that give a reason score higher: "lower the current, because undercut comes from too much heat at the toe" beats "lower the current".
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **WPS** is the written set of instructions that says exactly how a weld must be made so it will be sound. It is usually backed by a test weld that proved it works.

head: A WPS usually gives
Examples
rows: Single-V, 60° included angle, root face 1.5–2 mm, root gap 2.5–3 mm, with or without backing
Class and diameter for each run: for example 2.5 mm E7018 root, 3.2 mm E7018 fill and cap
Current range for each size; AC or DC and polarity; sometimes voltage and travel speed
Stringer or weave, number and order of runs, cleaning between runs
Any heat treatment, and the inspection required

head: Who
How they use the WPS
rows: Reads it before starting, sets up the joint and the machine to it, and stays inside its ranges
Checks the welder is qualified for it, the right electrodes are issued, and the fit-up, settings and preheat match it; records the checks; stops work that does not fit it

blocks.note: "It runs better at 160 A" is not a reason to leave the WPS range. Settings outside the range were never tested, so the weld is not covered by the procedure. If the range does not suit the job, the supervisor or engineer decides, not the welder.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Where a job calls for a qualified welder, the welder must have passed a test weld to the procedure (or one that covers it). The test proves that this person can make sound welds of that kind, in those positions and thicknesses. The record of it is the welder's qualification record.

ul: Thick steel draws heat away from the weld quickly, so the weld and the heat-affected zone (HAZ) cool fast. Fast cooling can make the HAZ hard and, with hydrogen, crack it.

**Preheat** (heating the joint before welding) slows the cooling. When a WPS gives a minimum preheat, heat the whole joint area evenly and **check the temperature** before welding, and keep it up while you weld. Jamaica's heat is not a preheat.
A **maximum interpass temperature** stops the joint getting too hot over many runs, which can coarsen the steel and lower its toughness. If the joint is too hot, wait for it to cool into range.

flow: Read the drawing and the WPS: joints, sizes, positions, electrodes, settings, temperatures, inspection
Check the welders' qualifications against the work
List and order the plate, electrodes (by class, size and quantity) and consumables
Plan the set-up: power supply or generator, machine, leads, screens, extraction, access
Plan the order of work and the distortion control
Set the checks: fit-up, settings, interpass, visual inspection, any tests
Brief the team; then record the work as it goes

sections.title: Safe working and leading safe work

head: Hazard
What a Level 3 welder knows
Controls
rows: The electrode, holder and work are live at the **open-circuit voltage** whenever the machine is on. Sweat and humidity make skin and clothing conduct far better.
Dry gloves and clothing; spares on hand
Never change an electrode with a bare or wet hand
Insulating mat on steel or damp floors
A **voltage-reducing device (VRD)** lowers the voltage at the holder when not welding: use it where fitted
If the return lead is clamped to building steel, a pipe or a chain, the welding current can find its own way back through other parts and overheat or damage them.
Clamp the return lead to the job itself, close to the weld
Never use pipework, building steel, lifting chains or machine bearings as part of the circuit
Welding fume harms the lungs over time; coatings make worse fume.
**Local extraction** that captures fume at the arc comes first
Respirators where extraction cannot do enough
Galvanised steel: zinc fume causes metal fume fever, so remove the coating or use extra controls
Fume and heat build up; oxygen can run low; escape is hard.
Forced ventilation with air, never oxygen
A **standby person** outside and a rescue plan
Hot-work permit where the site uses one
Containers that held fuel or chemicals
Vapour left inside a drum or tank can explode when heated, even when it looks empty.
Never weld or cut until a competent person has cleaned it and declared it safe

blocks.h: Site work with an engine-driven welder

ul: Check the machine, leads, holder and clamp before use; use leads thick enough for their length and current.
Place the machine so its **exhaust** blows away from people and work areas, never into a building or trench.
**Refuel only with the engine stopped and cool**, away from sparks, with no smoking.
Stop welding in rain unless the work area is covered and dry; stand on a dry board or mat.
Put up screens or barriers to protect other workers and the public from arc flash.
Position yourself so the breeze carries fume away from your face; use portable extraction or a respirator where fume cannot be controlled.

blocks.note: In Jamaica's heat a welder's shirt and gloves can be wet with sweat within minutes, and that is when tingles from the holder begin. Treat any tingle as a warning: stop, change into dry gloves, check the holder and leads, and report it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Before anyone strikes an arc: the leader's check

flow: PPE: helmet with the right shade, dry gloves, flame-resistant clothing, boots, glasses for chipping
Bay: screens closed, extraction on and working, floor dry, anything that burns cleared, extinguisher in place
Equipment: mains lead, machine, leads, holder and clamp undamaged; connections tight; return clamp on the job
Settings: AC or the right DC polarity, current within the WPS
Electrodes: right class and size, dry, issued from the store or oven
People: everyone knows the job, the hazards and who to call

sections.title: Power sources and the welding circuit

blocks.h: Why MMAW machines have a drooping output

blocks.p: MMAW power sources are **constant-current** machines, also said to have a **drooping** output: as the arc gets longer the voltage rises but the current changes only a little. Because the welder's hand can never hold the arc length exactly steady, this keeps the heat steady. (MIG machines are the opposite: constant voltage.)

When the machine is on and no arc is burning, the voltage between electrode and work is the **open-circuit voltage (OCV)**, often about 50–90 V, high enough to start the arc. Once the arc burns, the voltage falls to the **arc voltage**, about 20–30 V.

head: Type
How it works
Points to know
rows: Steps mains AC down to welding AC
Simple and tough; heavy; AC only
Transformer plus a rectifier to give DC
Heavy; AC and DC on some models
Electronics change the supply at high frequency, so the transformer is small
Light and easy to move to the job; good arc control; electronics need keeping clean and dry, like any machine
A diesel or petrol engine drives a welding generator
For sites with no supply; often also gives power for tools; exhaust and fuel hazards

blocks.p: The **duty cycle** is the percentage of a 10-minute period a machine can weld at a given current without overheating. 250 A at 30 % means 3 minutes welding and **7 minutes resting** in every 10 at 250 A.

At a lower current the machine can work for longer. A common approximation is: **duty cycle at the new current ≈ rated duty cycle × (rated current ÷ new current)²**, up to 100 %. For example, a machine rated 200 A at 40 % used at 160 A: 40 × (200 ÷ 160)² = 40 × 1.56 ≈ **62 %**, about 6 minutes in every 10. Use the maker's figures where they are given.

blocks.note: Duty cycles are rated at a set air temperature (often 40 °C). A machine in the sun or with blocked vents overheats sooner. If the thermal cut-out trips, leave the machine on so its fan cools it.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Leads must be thick enough for both the **current** and the **total length** of the circuit (electrode lead plus return lead). A cable too thin for its length and current gets hot and drops voltage, so the arc is weak and hard to hold. Use the maker's cable table.
Unroll leads fully, keep them out of walkways and off hot metal, and check connections are clean and tight: a loose joint gets hot and makes the arc unsteady.

head: Polarity
Connection
Typical use
rows: E7018, E6010 and most electrodes on DC; deeper penetration
Some rutile electrodes on thin metal; less heat into the work
Electrodes made for AC (such as E6013, E7018, E6011); no arc blow

blocks.p: An electrode run on the wrong polarity gives a harsh or unstable arc, spatter, poor fusion and porosity. If a normally smooth electrode suddenly runs badly, check the polarity against the packet (switch off before changing leads).

The welding current makes a magnetic field round the electrode, the work and the leads. Where the field is uneven (near the end of a joint, near a heavy mass of steel, in a corner, or because of where the return clamp is) it pushes the arc off line: **arc blow**. It is a DC problem; with AC the field keeps reversing.

ul: Change to AC, if the electrode allows it.
Move the return clamp, or use two clamps, or weld away from the clamp.
Weld towards a heavy tack or a finished weld; add tacks; use run-on and run-off tabs at the ends.
Tilt the electrode against the blow; hold a shorter arc; lower the current a little.
Have magnetism removed from badly magnetised steel.

blocks.p: In a class such as **E7018**: E = electrode; **70** = minimum tensile strength of the weld metal, 70 000 psi (about 480 MPa); the third digit is the positions (**1** = all positions, **2** = flat and horizontal fillets only); the third and fourth digits together give the coating type and the current (**18** = low-hydrogen with iron powder, AC or DCEP).

head: Electrode
Coating
Current
Arc and penetration
Storage
Typical jobs
rows: Forceful, digging arc; deep penetration; fast-freezing pool; much spatter
In its packet as the maker says; **never** oven-dried like low-hydrogen rods (its coating needs some moisture)
Root runs in pipe; dirty or rusty work
Soft, smooth arc; shallow to medium penetration; easy slag
Kept dry; dried at a low temperature if damp
Medium penetration; strong, tough, crack-resistant weld metal
Once opened: **holding oven**, then a heated **quiver** on the job
Structural steel, thick or restrained joints, steels that may crack
Rutile with a lot of iron powder
Very fast deposition; smooth, flat beads
Long flat and horizontal fillets only (third digit 2)

ul: Choose by the job: E7018 for a structural joint in thick steel that must resist cracking; E6010 for a pipe root; E6013 for light work.
Choose the **size** for the thickness, the joint and the position: too big an electrode makes a pool too large to control, especially vertical and overhead.
Match the electrode to the metal: a mild steel electrode on stainless steel gives a weld that rusts and can crack. Stainless needs a stainless electrode.
Damp flux causes porosity, a spattery arc and, with low-hydrogen electrodes, hydrogen cracking.

Low-hydrogen electrodes, once opened, live in a holding oven at the maker's temperature and go to the job in a heated quiver; those left out too long are re-dried only as the maker allows, or scrapped.
An electrode with **cracked, chipped or missing flux** is not used: it will not shield the arc properly.

head: Step
What it involves
rows: Dry, locked store; packets off the floor, labelled by class and size; oldest stock used first
Opened low-hydrogen electrodes kept at the maker's temperature; oven temperature checked and logged
Against the WPS for each job, only the amount needed; class, size, batch, job and welder recorded
Heated quivers for low-hydrogen electrodes; stubs into a metal bin
Unused electrodes back to the store or oven at the end of the shift; re-dried or scrapped as the maker says
The right electrode in good condition on every weld, and every weld traceable to its electrode batch if a problem appears

head: Feature
Typical figure (always follow the WPS)
Why it matters
rows: Wide enough for the electrode to reach the root and fuse the side walls; any wider wastes weld metal and time and adds distortion
Too thin: burn-through and too much penetration; too thick: the root does not penetrate
About 2.5–3 mm, set with a spacer
Too wide: burn-through and icicles; too small: lack of root penetration
A step (mismatch) gives an uneven root and stress

ul: Clean the bevels and about 25 mm each side to bright metal.
A **backing bar** or strip under the root lets it be fully welded without falling through. A steel backing strip is welded in and stays; it must be the steel the WPS names.

**Run-on and run-off tabs** are small plates tacked at the ends of the joint, prepared like it, so the weld can start and finish off the job. Start and stop faults (porosity, craters, poor fusion, arc blow) end up on the tabs, which are cut off afterwards, and the weld is full size right to the plate edges.
Tack at the ends (or on the tabs) and in the middle as needed; set a small **pre-set** so the plates finish flat; clean the tacks and grind their ends to a taper.
Cut the edge of the upright plate square so it sits tight on the base plate: a gap under it reduces the real weld size.
Tack at each end, check the upright with a square, and clean the tacks.
Check the drawing for the leg length or throat, and the number of runs the WPS gives.

blocks.p: Check the bevel angle, root face, root gap and alignment with gauges, the cleanliness, the tacks and the squareness, and record it. A fit-up fault corrected now costs minutes; found after welding it costs a cut-out and a re-weld.

sections.title: Welding method: positions and multi-run welds

ul: Vertical and overhead welds usually need a little less current than the same joint flat (often about 10–15 % less, within the WPS range).

Weld **vertical-up** with E7018 and for full fusion on plate: use a slight weave and **pause at each side** to fill the edges and prevent undercut. Downhill welding is fast but can leave lack of fusion on plate, and E7018 is not made for it.
Overhead: small electrodes, a very short arc, small stringer runs; stand to the side with head and shoulders covered.

head: Run
How
Purpose
rows: Smaller electrode (often 2.5 mm), arc kept in the root, a small keyhole kept just ahead of the pool
Even penetration bead on the underside, fused into both root faces
Next run, at a slightly higher current, straight after the root is cleaned
Burns out slag trapped along the edges of the root bead and re-melts its surface
Stringers or a narrow weave, built up evenly; every run cleaned
Fill the groove with sound, well-fused metal
Slight, even **reinforcement** that blends smoothly into the plate at the toes, with no undercut

ul: **Clean every run**: chip, wire brush, and grind any high spots or slag lines. Slag left in is trapped as an inclusion.
Check the interpass temperature where the WPS gives one.
Restart just ahead of the crater, on the joint line, then come back to fill it.
Fill every crater before breaking the arc: open craters crack.
With E7018, strike ahead on the joint line and move back, with a short arc, to avoid porosity at the start.

blocks.note: More reinforcement is not more strength. A tall cap (more than about 3 mm, or the limit in the code) with sharp toes concentrates stress at the toes, where cracks start under changing loads. It also wastes electrodes and time.
blocks.label: Remember

ol: Run 1 into the root, electrode at about 45° between the plates, fusing into both plates.
Run 2 on the **bottom** plate, overlapping about half of run 1, electrode aimed a little more at the base plate.
Run 3 against the **upright** plate, overlapping run 2, electrode aimed a little more at the upright, to give equal legs and a flat or slightly convex face with no undercut on the upright.

blocks.p: Clean each run before the next. Lean the electrode about 10–20° in the direction of travel. Undercut along the top toe usually means too much current or too long an arc; lower the current and shorten the arc.

head: What you work out
Formula
Worked example
rows: Length of weld ÷ length laid per minute
3.6 m of weld at 120 mm a minute = 3 600 ÷ 120 = 30 minutes
Rest time on the duty cycle
35 % at full rating: 6.5 minutes rest in every 10
Mass needed ÷ mass per packet, always rounded **up**
5.2 kg in 2.5 kg packets = 2.08, so 3 packets

blocks.note: Write the formula first, put the numbers in, then check the answer makes sense. Heat inputs for MMAW are usually between about 0.5 and 3 kJ/mm; if you get 15, you have probably missed the × 1 000.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Heat input depends on the voltage (set mostly by your arc length), the current and the travel speed. A wide weave is slow travel, so it raises heat input.
**Too much**: a big, slow-cooling weld area with coarse grain, more distortion, and sometimes lower toughness.
**Too little**: fast cooling, which in thick or higher-carbon steel can give hard zones and cracking, and can leave lack of fusion.
A WPS may give a heat input range. Keep to it by holding the current in range, a steady arc length, a steady travel speed, and the bead type the WPS gives.

head: Fault
Main causes
How it is found
Prevention
rows: Lack of fusion (side wall or between runs)
Current too low; wrong electrode angle; travel too fast; weave not reaching the edges
Bend tests, fillet breaks, ultrasonic testing
Correct current, angle and speed; aim the arc at both sides
Root gap too small; root face too large; current too low; electrode too big
Visual check of the underside; bend and break tests; radiography
Correct gap and root face; smaller root electrode
Root gap too wide; root face too thin; current too high; travel too slow
Poor cleaning between runs; deep valleys at the root edges; current too low
Clean every run; hot pass; good bead shape
Damp electrodes; oil, paint, rust or zinc; long arc; arc blow; long arc at E7018 starts
Dry electrodes; clean metal; short arc; strike ahead and move back
Hydrogen (damp electrodes, dirty plate), a hard HAZ from fast cooling (no preheat on thick steel), restraint; may appear hours later
Visual, magnetic particle or ultrasonic testing after a waiting time
Dry low-hydrogen electrodes; clean joints; preheat as the WPS gives
Current too high; long arc; wrong angle; no pause at the edges
Lower current; short arc; correct angle; pause at the edges
Too few runs; travel too fast
Follow the WPS run plan; check legs as you go
Too many or too large cap runs
Plan the cap; blend the toes

ul: Visual inspection comes first, on every weld, once the slag is off: size, profile, toes, cracks, porosity, craters, arc strikes, spatter, root penetration where it can be seen.
A **fillet gauge** measures leg length and throat; a weld gauge measures butt-weld **reinforcement** and undercut.
An undersize weld does not meet the drawing: record it and add the run(s) needed, to the WPS, then measure again.

head: Test
Kind
What it shows
Used on
rows: A strip bent round a former must not crack open: soundness, fusion and ductility
Test pieces for welder and procedure qualification
A cut, smoothed and etched face shows fusion, penetration and the run layout
The broken face shows lack of fusion, slag and porosity inside
Cracks open to the surface, on any non-porous metal (stainless steel included)
Cracks at or just below the surface, using a magnet and fine iron powder; **only on magnetic steels**
Faults inside the weld, found with high-frequency sound
Faults inside the weld (porosity, slag, lack of fusion) on a film or screen
Butt welds where the specification asks

blocks.note: Destructive tests destroy the sample, so they are used on test pieces. Non-destructive tests are used on the actual job, on the share of welds the specification sets, after visual inspection.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Mark and photograph the fault; stop the item being used
Raise a non-conformance report: the weld, the fault, its size and position, how it was found
Plan the repair with the supervisor: remove cracks completely and prove them gone (PT or MT) before welding
Weld the repair to the WPS (with preheat if it says), by a qualified welder, with dry electrodes
Inspect and test the repair again; record the method, the welder and the results, and close the report

blocks.p: Repairs are written into the job's weld records so they can be inspected and traced later.

ul: Do the leader's check before any arc is struck (see Safe working).
**Watch before you correct.** A rough, spattery bead is often an arc length that keeps changing; a groove at the toe is often current or angle. Find the cause from what the trainee does.
Coach one change at a time, show it, let the trainee try on scrap, then check the next weld.
Keep settings inside the WPS, and explain why.
Record what was taught, the faults found and any near misses.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain what a WPS contains and how the welder and the supervisor each use it.
I can explain why welders are qualified, and why preheat and interpass limits are set.
I can control shock, stray current, fume, confined-space, fire and site hazards, and check a bay before welding.
I can explain constant-current output, OCV, machine types, duty cycle, cable size and polarity.
I can explain arc blow and the ways to control it.
I can compare E6010, E6013, E7018 and E7024, read their codes, and choose one for a job.
I can run an electrode store, oven and issue system.
I can prepare and fit a single-V butt and a tee joint to a WPS, with backing and tabs where needed.
I can weld root, hot pass, fill and cap runs, and a three-run fillet, in position.
I can work out travel speed, heat input, arc time, throat and leg sizes, duty cycle, quantities and costs.
I can name the common faults, their causes, how they are found and how to prevent them.
I can explain destructive and non-destructive tests and choose a suitable one.
I can plan and record a repair.
I can supervise and coach trainees in the welding bay.

terms: Arc blow
The arc pushed off its line by magnetic forces, mostly on DC
Backing bar or strip
A bar or strip under a butt joint so the root can be fully welded
Cap
The final run or runs on the face of a multi-run weld
Constant-current (drooping) output
A power source whose current changes little when the arc length changes
Duty cycle
The percentage of 10 minutes a machine can weld at a given current
Fillet gauge
A gauge for measuring the leg length and throat of a fillet weld
Heat-affected zone (HAZ)
Parent metal changed by the heat of welding but not melted
Heat input
Arc energy per millimetre of weld, in kJ/mm
Hot pass
The run straight after the root, which burns out slag along the root edges
Interpass temperature
The temperature of the joint just before the next run
Magnetic particle testing
Finding surface cracks in magnetic steel with a magnet and fine iron powder
Open-circuit voltage (OCV)
The voltage at the electrode when the machine is on but not welding
Preheat
Heating the joint before welding to slow its cooling
Quiver
A small heated container that keeps low-hydrogen electrodes dry on the job
Reinforcement
Weld metal standing above the plate surface on the face of a butt weld
Root face
The flat land left at the bottom of a bevel
Root gap
The space between the parts at the root of a joint
Run-on and run-off tabs
Small plates at the ends of a joint so the weld can start and finish off the job
Ultrasonic testing
Finding defects inside a weld with high-frequency sound
VRD
Voltage-reducing device: lowers the voltage at the holder when not welding
WPS
Welding procedure specification: the written instructions for making a weld

c1.title: A skip-bin frame in Bull Bay
c1.text: At a shop in Bull Bay, St Andrew, Rajay is welding single-V butt joints in 10 mm plate for a skip-bin frame, flat, to a WPS that gives a 60° included angle, a 1.5–2 mm root face and a 2.5–3 mm root gap. On his first joint, weld metal hangs in drops below the root; the root faces were ground almost to a knife edge and the gap is about 4 mm. His cap stands about 5 mm proud with sharp toes. The WPS also calls for run-on and run-off tabs.

c2.title: Fencing a cricket ground in Albert Town
c2.text: A crew is welding steel fence panels and 8 mm plate brackets at a cricket ground in Albert Town, Trelawny, with an engine-driven welder. Its rating plate says 200 A at 40 %; the crew is welding at about 160 A. The brackets have vertical joints to be welded with E7018 electrodes. By mid-afternoon the welder's fuel is low and the engine is hot.

c3.title: A machine base in Bog Walk
c3.text: Tamika is welding a machine base for a juice factory in Bog Walk, St Catherine, from 10 mm plate. The tee joints get three-run 8 mm fillet welds in the horizontal (2F) position. On a few lighter joints the drawing asks only for a 4.2 mm throat. The job needs about 14 m of the three-run fillet, which uses about 0.6 kg of electrodes per metre; the electrodes cost J$2 100 per kg.

c4.title: Checking kitchen work at a hotel in Negril
c4.text: Fabian, a Level 3 welder, is checking welds on a kitchen refit at a hotel in Negril, Westmoreland. There are stainless steel sink frames, mild steel supports for the canopy, and butt-welded mild steel pipe for a hot-water line. A trial tee joint, made by a new welder, has been broken open in a fillet break test.

c5.title: An evening class in May Pen
c5.text: Odane, a Level 3 trainee, is helping an instructor supervise an evening MMAW class at a training centre in May Pen, Clarendon. One trainee has picked E7024 electrodes for a set of vertical fillet welds because "they lay down metal fast". Another is running E7018 on a DC machine; his arc is harsh and unsteady and his welds are porous, though the electrodes came straight from the oven. The packet says "AC or DC+".

questions.q: What most likely caused the drops of weld metal hanging below Rajay's root?
o: The root faces were too thick and the gap too small
The root faces were too thin and the gap too wide
The electrodes had been kept in the oven too long
The included angle was too narrow for the electrode
questions.why: A knife-edge root face and a 4 mm gap give the root nothing to hold the pool, so it drops through as icicles (excess penetration). Grinding the root face to 1.5–2 mm and setting the gap to the WPS with a spacer cures it.

questions.q: After the root is cleaned, why does the WPS call for a hot pass?
o: To burn out slag along the root's edges
To cool the root quickly so that it does not crack
To fill the joint in one run and save electrodes
To give the cap a higher, stronger reinforcement
questions.why: The edges of a root bead leave narrow valleys where slag gets trapped. A slightly hotter run straight after cleaning re-melts the root surface and floats that slag out before the fill runs bury it.

questions.q: What is wrong with Rajay's 5 mm high cap?
o: Nothing: a taller cap makes the joint stronger
It is too low and must have another run added
It is too high, so the root will not have penetrated
Too high: its sharp toes concentrate stress
questions.why: Extra reinforcement adds no strength. A tall cap with sharp toes makes a notch where stress gathers and cracks can start under changing loads; the cap should be slight and even and blend into the plate.

questions.q: What are the run-on and run-off tabs for?
o: They let the welder test the current before each run
They hold the plates in line in place of the tacks
They stop the plates from distorting as they cool
They keep start and stop faults off the joint
questions.why: The weld starts and finishes on the tabs, so porosity, craters, poor fusion and arc blow at the ends end up there. The tabs are cut off afterwards, leaving a full-size weld right to the plate edges.

questions.q: Roughly what duty cycle can the crew expect at 160 A?
o: 40 %, the same as at 200 A
About 50 %
About 62 %
100 %, as 160 A is well below 200 A
questions.why: A common approximation is rated duty × (rated current ÷ new current)²: 40 × (200 ÷ 160)² = 40 × 1.56 ≈ 62 %, about 6 minutes of welding in every 10. Use the maker's figures where given; hot sun lowers it.

questions.q: How should the welder be refuelled?
o: With the engine stopped and cooled, away from sparks and smoking
Quickly, with the engine running so the welding is not held up
With the engine idling slowly, so it uses less fuel while filling
With the engine running but the welding switched off at the panel
questions.why: Fuel spilt on a hot engine or exhaust, or near sparks, can catch fire. Stop the engine, let it cool, refuel away from the welding with no smoking, and wipe up spills before restarting.

questions.q: How should the vertical joints on the 8 mm brackets be welded with E7018?
o: Downhill, quickly, so the pool cannot run
Downhill for the root and uphill for the cap
In short sideways dabs across the joint
Uphill, pausing at the edges
questions.why: Welding uphill lets the heat fuse properly into the plate; pausing at each edge fills the toes and stops undercut. E7018 is not a downhill electrode, and downhill welds on plate risk lack of fusion.

questions.q: Where should Tamika place the second and third runs of each three-run fillet?
o: Both on top of the first run, one directly over the other
The second on the upright plate, the third on the base plate
The second on the base plate, the third against the upright
Both down the middle, each wider than the run before it
questions.why: Run 1 goes into the root. Run 2 lies on the base plate, overlapping about half of run 1; run 3 lies against the upright, overlapping run 2. This gives equal legs and avoids undercut and sagging on the upright.

questions.q: What leg length gives the 4.2 mm throat the drawing asks for on the lighter joints?
o: About 3 mm
About 4.2 mm
About 6 mm
About 8.4 mm
questions.why: For an equal-leg, flat-faced fillet the throat is about 0.7 × the leg, so the leg = 4.2 ÷ 0.7 = 6 mm.

questions.q: What will the electrodes for the 14 m of three-run fillet cost?
questions.why: Mass = 14 m × 0.6 kg/m = 8.4 kg. Cost = 8.4 × J$2 100 = J$17 640. Order whole packets, rounding up, plus some spare.

questions.q: Which method should Fabian use to look for surface cracks in the stainless steel sink frames?
o: Magnetic particle testing
Dye penetrant testing
A hardness test
A fillet break test
questions.why: Magnetic particle testing needs a magnetic steel, and most stainless steels used in kitchens are not magnetic. Dye penetrant works on any non-porous metal and shows cracks open to the surface without damaging the job.

questions.q: To look for porosity and slag inside the butt welds on the hot-water line, which kind of test is suitable?
o: A visual check of the weld caps
Dye penetrant on the outside of the welds
A bend test on a section cut from the line
Radiography or ultrasonic testing
questions.why: Faults inside a butt weld cannot be seen from the surface. Radiography or ultrasonics find them without cutting the pipe; a bend test would destroy the part, and visual and penetrant checks show only the surface.

questions.q: The broken trial fillet shows that the weld never fused into the root. Which change should Fabian coach first?
o: Aim into the root, current up within the range
Weave wider at the root so the weld covers both plates
Use a bigger electrode so the root fills in fewer runs
Hold a longer arc so the heat spreads into the corner
questions.why: Lack of root fusion comes from too little heat at the root: low current, an arc not aimed into the corner, or travelling too fast. Aiming at the root at about 45° with the current up within the WPS range gives fusion into both plates.

questions.q: Why should the trainee not use E7024 for the vertical fillet welds?
o: It must be run on DCEN, which the bay machines lack
The 2 in it means flat and horizontal fillets only
It needs a holding oven at a much higher temperature
It is a cellulosic electrode, made for pipe root runs
questions.why: In E7024 the third digit 2 means flat and horizontal fillet positions only. Its heavy iron-powder coating makes a large, fluid pool that cannot be held on a vertical joint. An all-position electrode (third digit 1) is needed.

questions.q: What should Odane check first about the second trainee's E7018 problem?
o: Whether the plate is thick enough for E7018 electrodes
Whether the machine is set to DC+, as the packet says
Whether the oven is hot enough to dry the electrodes
Whether the trainee has picked the right filter shade
questions.why: A harsh, unsteady arc and porosity from electrodes that are known to be dry points to the wrong polarity. With the machine switched off, connect the electrode lead to + as "DC+" on the packet requires.

questions.q: Pass A is welded at 22 V, 120 A and 150 mm/min; pass B at 24 V, 110 A and 200 mm/min. Which has the higher heat input?
o: Pass B, because its voltage is higher
Pass A, at about 1.06 kJ/mm against 0.79
They are equal, as volts × amps is the same
Pass B, at about 1.06 kJ/mm against 0.79
questions.why: A: 22 × 120 × 60 ÷ 150 000 ≈ 1.06 kJ/mm. B: 24 × 110 × 60 ÷ 200 000 ≈ 0.79 kJ/mm. Volts × amps are equal (2 640 W), but A travels more slowly, so each millimetre gets more heat.

questions.q: Why is a single-V butt usually bevelled to about 60° included, and not 90°?
o: 60° reaches the root; 90° only adds weld and distortion
A 90° V is too narrow for the electrode to reach the root
60° is the only angle a grinder can cut accurately on plate
A wider V always gives lack of fusion on the side walls
questions.why: About 60° lets the electrode reach the root and fuse the side walls. A wider V must be filled with much more weld metal, which takes longer, costs more and shrinks more, so distortion grows. Too narrow a V risks lack of fusion.

questions.q: A farmer brings an empty 200-litre drum that held diesel and asks for a bracket to be welded onto it. What should you do?
o: Weld it quickly with the bung out, so any vapour can escape
Fill it with water first, then weld near the top of the drum
Not until a competent person declares it safe
Weld it at a low current so that it does not get hot inside
questions.why: Diesel vapour and residue left inside can explode when the drum is heated, even when it looks empty and the bung is out. It must be cleaned and declared safe by a competent person before any hot work, or a new bracket fixed another way.

questions.q: Why does a WPS often ask for preheat on a thick carbon steel joint welded with low-hydrogen electrodes?
o: To make the slag easier to remove between the runs
To burn off the mill scale so the plate needs no cleaning
Low-hydrogen electrodes will only strike on warm steel
To slow the fast cooling that thick plate causes
questions.why: Thick steel draws heat out of the joint quickly, and fast cooling can harden the HAZ and, with any hydrogen, crack it. Preheat slows the cooling. Heat the whole joint area evenly and check the temperature before welding.

questions.q: A fillet gauge shows 6 mm legs on a joint the drawing marks as 8 mm. What should happen?
o: Record it, build it up to size, and re-measure
Accept it, as 6 mm is close enough on an 8 mm fillet
Grind it flush and weld it again as a single run
Paint it, as the coating will build it up to size
questions.why: A 6 mm fillet has a throat of about 4.2 mm against about 5.6 mm for 8 mm, so it is a quarter weaker. It is recorded as a fault, cleaned and built up to size to the WPS, then measured again.
